summary: The English of 4:19-4:22 is faithful and keeps the sayings brief. The main faults are in the word analysis: the senses were filled mechanically with '1', so most verbs name no binyan and some twenty tokens point at the wrong homograph (Gath, Heshbon, Dan, Baal, Bajith, Adam, 'menstruation', 'bird of prey', 'boundary', 'where?'). These are re-keyed to the right Jastrow entries or have their senses removed. In the text: 'He is about to judge' is corrected to 'destined to judge' (Bartenura, Rambam). Two rulings are corrected: Bartenura on 4:20, where גִּרְסַת הַיַּלְדוּת was misread, and Rambam on מִקַּח שֹׁחַד. A false claim about the Masoretic text of Prov. 24:18 is removed. The model morphology has wrong binyanim (לְהֵחָיוֹת and לִדּוֹן are Niphal), verbal adjectives parsed as participles (יִלּוֹדִים, עָתִיד), the verb וְרַע parsed as an adjective, and several lemmas wrong.

patches.value: Elisha son of Avuyah says: One who learns as a child, to what is he compared? To ink written on new paper. And one who learns as an old man, to what is he compared? To ink written on erased paper. Rabbi Yose son of Yehudah, a man of Kefar HaBavli, says: One who learns from the young, to what is he compared? To one who eats unripe grapes and drinks wine from its winepress. And one who learns from the old, to what is he compared? To one who eats ripe grapes and drinks aged wine. Rabbi says: Do not look at the jar, but at what is in it. There is a new jar full of old wine, and an old one in which there is not even new.
patches.reason: מִגִּתּוֹ: the suffix is the wine's: wine still from its vat, with its lees mixed in (Bartenura). 'his winepress' reads as the drinker's own press.

patches.value: He used to say: Those who are born are to die, and the dead are to be revived, and the living are to be judged; to know, to make known, and to come to know that He is God, He is the Former, He is the Creator, He is the Discerner, He is the Judge, He is the Witness, He is the Plaintiff, and He is destined to judge. Blessed is He, before whom there is no injustice, no forgetfulness, no partiality, and no taking of bribes, for everything is His. And know that everything is according to the reckoning. And do not let your impulse assure you that Sheol is a place of refuge for you, for against your will you were formed, and against your will you were born, and against your will you live, and against your will you die, and against your will you are destined to give judgment and account before the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.

patches.value: The Hebrew leaves open who 'knows', 'makes known' and 'comes to know'; the English keeps the three infinitives bare, and Bartenura's glosses (from others, to others, from oneself) are given in the commentary entries. אֵל is read as 'God', following Bartenura's silence and Rabbeinu Yonah's gloss 'strong, mighty' recorded in the apparatus; the pack lexicon links token 14 to אַל ('not'), which is not the word, and its sense is removed. עָתִיד לָדוּן is 'is destined to judge' (Bartenura: in the world to come), the same word as עָתִיד לִתֵּן below. שֶׁהַכֹּל לְפִי הַחֶשְׁבּוֹן: 'according to the reckoning'; Bartenura gives the sum of small coins, which the English does not add. In the line on the impulse, שְׁאוֹל is Sheol; the pack lemma (Saul) is wrong, and its sense is removed.
patches.reason: The note must follow the corrected English ('destined to judge') and the removed senses.

patches.value: Rambam: 'to know, to make known and to be known' refers to those to be born, those born now who will die, and those who will live after death; from these three classes one learns that He is the Former and the Creator. 'The Judge' is His judging now, in life and death; 'destined to judge' is the judgment, with reward and punishment, of those who live in the world to come. 'No taking of bribes' does not mean a bribe to pervert judgment, which is absurd of God, but that He does not let many good deeds buy off one transgression: He punishes the one and rewards the others; 'no partiality' means even the great are punished for a small sin (Moses). 'Against your will' lists only natural events without choice; it does not say 'against your will you sin'.
patches.reason: The summary reduced Rambam on מִקַּח שֹׁחַד to 'as the Torah says', when he expressly denies the plain sense of bribery ('ואין ענינו שלא יקח שחד להטות הדין') and explains it as good deeds not offsetting a sin; it also omitted his point that עַל כָּרְחֲךָ covers natural events only.

value: Variant: Vilna reads לידון (4:22.9), הדיין (4:22.22), שוחד (4:22.44), ליתן (4:22.78) for the base spellings.

Rambam (normative): מִקַּח שֹׁחַד does not mean a bribe to pervert judgment, but that a man's thousand good deeds do not buy off one transgression; מַשּׂוֹא פָנִים, that the great are punished for a small matter. He cites the Torah's לֹא יִשָּׂא פָנִים וְלֹא יִקַּח שֹׁחַד (Deut. 10:17).
Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative): אֵל from the sense 'mighty' (as in 2 Kings 24:15, 'the mighty of the land').
Rabbeinu Yonah: 'Former' is the start of the work and 'Creator' its completion.
Rabbeinu Yonah on 'let your impulse assure you': do not say that Sheol is a place of refuge, as the heretics say, 'in the world to come there is neither judgment nor judge'.
patches.reason: The Rambam line said 'No taking of bribes is as the Torah says', which inverts his point: he rejects the plain sense of bribery for God.

הַיִּלּוֹדִים is the plural of the verbal adjective יִלּוֹד 'born'; a Niphal participle would be נוֹלָדִים (as נוֹלָד in this mishnah).
לְהֵחָיוֹת is the Niphal infinitive (הֵחָיוֹת, like הֵרָאוֹת), 'to be revived'; a Hiphil infinitive would be לְהַחֲיוֹת.
לִדּוֹן is the Niphal infinitive contracted from לְהִדּוֹן, with the ד doubled ('to be judged'); the Qal is לָדוּן, as in 4:22.30.

verdicts.comment: A note on Samuel's habit of quoting the verse; it does not bear on the English.
The English has the anger turn away from the enemy; Bartenura's transfer onto the gloater is recorded in the ruling.
Bartenura: לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא. 'About to judge' made it imminent; patched to 'destined to judge'.
Rambam's 'destined to judge' is the future judgment, which the patched English now carries; his reading of מִקַּח שֹׁחַד is an interpretation of the same words and the patched summary records it.
